_about: Known attack campaigns, shipped inside every signed ScamHunter release so they reach every user under the same signature check as the code. Addresses are the attacker's; domains and IPs are attacker infrastructure, not the websites that were hit. Each entry names its public sources.

campaigns.name: OPTIMJACK
campaigns.kind: address-swapping script on trusted websites (crypto clipper + card skimmer)
campaigns.summary: Scripts served from Optimizely's CDN (cdn.optimizely.com) to 186+ large websites were altered to load malware from 1688360.cc. On pages with words like 'wallet', 'deposit' or 'send', it swapped crypto addresses for the attacker's (in page text, form fields, copy-paste and the clipboard), stole card numbers and cookies, and sent older iPhones to an exploit stage.
campaigns.victim_note: Your payment went to an address that was swapped on a website you trusted. You did nothing wrong: the address you copied was replaced before you pasted it. Every swapped address passes its checksum, so wallets accept it.
user_advice: Before sending crypto, check the address on your hardware wallet's screen (or read it back) against the address the site shows, not what you pasted.
If you entered a card number on an affected site on Nov 16-17, 2026, ask your card issuer for a new card.
On an iPhone or iPad running iOS 18.6 or earlier that visited affected sites, update iOS.

campaigns.name: Binance heist (TraderTraitor)
campaigns.kind: exchange theft by North Korean state hackers; these are the laundering wallets
campaigns.summary: About $6.4 billion was stolen from Binance hot wallets on Oct 29, 2026, the largest crypto theft on record. The FBI attributes it to North Korea's TraderTraitor group and published 628 addresses (608 Ethereum, 19 Bitcoin, 1 Solana) for exchanges and wallets to block. Billions were frozen by issuers and exchanges within days.
campaigns.victim_note: This address is on the FBI's list of wallets used to launder the Binance theft. Don't send anything to it. If you received funds from it, your exchange may freeze them: contact the exchange's support through its app, and keep records.
user_advice: Binance users did not need to do anything to be repaid. Any message offering 'compensation', a 'refund' or a 'reconciliation payout' for a fee is a scam.
Never send crypto to receive crypto, verify a wallet, or unlock a payout.
Reach Binance or Trust Wallet only through the official app or by typing the address yourself.

verified.source_copy: FBI list as published in ShapeShift's open-source screening code (commit 977b325, Nov 1, 2026), which cites the FBI alert; fbi.gov refused automated download, so it was not bypassed
verified.cross_check: all 628 match two further independent public copies (github.com/omiiii274/binance-hack-tracer, github.com/fdddf/chainsentinel)
verified.checksums: 608 Ethereum (all EIP-55 checksums valid), 19 Bitcoin (bech32 valid), 1 Solana (valid); no duplicates

campaigns.name: Fake Binance compensation
campaigns.kind: phishing and advance-fee scams riding on the Binance heist
campaigns.summary: Within days of the Binance theft, fake messages appeared: a '$150 compensation reward' shown in fake screenshots; a 'SAFU Reconciliation Desk' email promising a Bitcoin payout for a 0.0042 BTC 'wallet-verification fee'; and 'Binance Hack Also Impacts Trust Wallet Users' emails telling people to verify their wallet before Nov 7 or be suspended.
campaigns.victim_note: If you paid a 'verification fee' or entered a recovery phrase on one of these pages, assume the wallet is compromised: move what's left to a new wallet made on a clean device, and report to IC3.
user_advice: Never pay a fee to receive compensation, a refund or a payout.
Never 'verify' a wallet from a link in an email or text.
Never type your recovery phrase into any website.

campaigns.name: FaceStealer
campaigns.kind: fake video meetings by North Korean hackers (hijacked contacts, recorded webcam video, 'fix your audio' malware)
campaigns.summary: FBI FLASH (Nov 12, 2026): North Korean hackers take over someone's Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack or Discord, invite that person's contacts to a video call on a fake Zoom or Teams site, play secretly recorded webcam video of the real person, then claim an audio problem and have the target run an 'update' or paste a command. That installs malware that steals wallets, cookies and keystrokes. Over $400 million stolen in about 18 months; crypto workers and open-source developers are prime targets.
campaigns.victim_note: If you ran a script or installed an 'update' during a video call, assume the computer and every wallet on it are compromised.
user_advice: Join meetings from the official Zoom or Teams app with the meeting code, not from a link in a chat.
Never run a script, paste a command or install an 'update' to fix a call. Hang up and rejoin from the official app.
Keep your webcam off until you've confirmed the person is really there, and confirm unusual invites by a different channel.
If you ran something: from a clean device, move crypto to a new wallet with a new recovery phrase, change passwords, sign out all sessions, and report to IC3 with the keyword FaceStealer.

campaigns.name: Midterm election scams
campaigns.kind: fake campaign 'investment pools', fake PACs, fake merchandise, fake voter-registration texts
campaigns.summary: FBI PSA I-101526-3 (Oct 15, 2026): scammers sell 'campaign investment pools' that supposedly pay out when a candidate wins, pose as PACs and keep donations, sell election merchandise that never ships, and text people that they aren't registered to vote, with a link that steals personal information.
campaigns.victim_note: Campaign donations are never an investment and never pay a return.
user_advice: Check your registration only at vote.gov or your state's election site.
Check a PAC on the FEC website before giving.
Don't click registration links in unexpected texts.

sources.title: FBI PSA I-101526-3: Scammers Exploit 2026 U.S. Midterm Election to Perpetrate Multiple Fraud Schemes

campaigns.name: Lunex Stealer (fake 'verify you are human')
campaigns.kind: ClickFix: hacked websites show a fake Cloudflare check that tells you to paste a PowerShell command
campaigns.summary: CERT-UA (reported Oct 6, 2026): over 100 legitimate websites were altered to show a fake Cloudflare 'verify you are human' page telling visitors to copy and run a PowerShell command. It installs Lunex Stealer, which takes passwords, login sessions and crypto wallets, sometimes with a fake 'Microsoft Office Word Editor' browser extension. The same trick (ClickFix) is behind much of this month's malware worldwide.
campaigns.victim_note: If you pasted a command from a web page, assume passwords, logged-in sessions and wallets on that computer are exposed.
user_advice: No real website ever asks you to paste anything into PowerShell, the Run box (Win+R) or Terminal to prove you're human.
Check your browser extensions for anything you don't recognise, especially one named like an Office tool.
